questions.prompt: A “pure hypothetical” / chain argument, as Hicks sets it up, links:
choices: A Only categorical A/E/I/O sentences.
B If P then Q, if Q then R, therefore if P then R (as many consistent links as needed).
C A majority’s beliefs to a conclusion.
D An insult to a person with a claim.
questions.explain: All constituent propositions are hypotheticals; P links to Q, Q to R, so P to R.

questions.prompt: Hicks symbolizes inclusive either-or with a wedge (v). “If and only if” is explained as:
choices: A A single atomic category with no structure.
B If P then Q and if Q then P—two hypotheticals combined.
C Always equivalent to denying the antecedent.
D A type of informal subjectivism.
questions.explain: P iff Q unpacks as (if P then Q) and (if Q then P).

questions.prompt: In the truth-functional treatment of “and,” which situation makes “Peter and Quincy are coming” false?
choices: A Only when both come.
B When Quincy shows and Peter does not (and likewise other failures of both conjuncts).
C Never—conjunctions cannot be false.
D Only when the sentence is in Latin.
questions.explain: If one comes and the other doesn’t, or neither comes, the conjunction is false.

questions.prompt: The constructive dilemma, as labeled here, is essentially:
choices: A Two modus ponens steps packaged with an either-or.
B An ad hominem against both disjuncts.
C Begging the question in 25 pages.
D Induction from pasta to all pasta.
questions.explain: Either P or R; if P then Q; if R then S; therefore Q or S—two affirming-the-antecedent moves together.

questions.prompt: Why can mapping true/false onto 1/0 matter practically, on Hicks’s account?
choices: A It proves Hegel was a universal logician.
B Binary can be instantiated in on/off electrical switches, so logic underwrites computing hardware.
C It shows informal fallacies cannot be named.
D It replaces modus tollens with majority vote.
questions.explain: T/F ↔ 1/0 maps onto electrical switches on/off; combinations of lines and switches machine-represent logical structure.
